title: Recursion: Factorial
oneLiner: A function that calls itself, with a stopping condition -- the call stack does the bookkeeping.
keyTakeaway: Recursion is just the call stack (the list of function calls that have started but not yet returned, newest on top) keeping track of "what to do when this call finally returns" for you. Every recursive function needs a base case that stops the recursion -- without one, it's an infinite loop that happens to crash with a stack overflow (the memory reserved for the call stack running out) instead of hanging forever.
explanation: factorial(n) = n x (n-1) x (n-2) x ... x 1, and it has a natural recursive definition: factorial(n) = n * factorial(n - 1), with factorial(0) = 1 as the base case (the thing that stops the recursion). Each call to factorial(n) can't finish until factorial(n - 1) returns -- so calls pile up on the call stack (factorial(5) waiting on factorial(4) waiting on factorial(3)...) until the base case is hit, and then they unwind, each one multiplying its own n by the result it got back. Step through the visualization to see the stack grow (calling down to the base case) and then shrink (returning back up, computing as it goes). Watch out for the base case being wrong in either direction: missing it entirely means infinite recursion (stack overflow), and an off-by-one base case can do the same: stopping only at n == 1 works for factorial(5), but factorial(0) (which this lesson tests) then calls factorial(-1), factorial(-2), ... and never reaches it. A base case of n <= 1 catches both 0 and 1.

starterCode.python:
def factorial(n):
    # TODO: base case -- if n is 0, return 1.
    # Otherwise, return n * factorial(n - 1).
    return 0

visualizationSteps.message: factorial(5) -- not the base case, so call factorial(4) and wait for it to return.
factorial(4) -- not the base case, so call factorial(3) and wait for it to return.
factorial(3) -- not the base case, so call factorial(2) and wait for it to return.
factorial(2) -- not the base case, so call factorial(1) and wait for it to return.
factorial(1) -- not the base case, so call factorial(0) and wait for it to return.
factorial(0) -- base case reached. Return 1 without recursing further.
factorial(0) returned. factorial(1) computes 1 * 1 = 1 and returns.
factorial(1) returned. factorial(2) computes 2 * 1 = 2 and returns.
factorial(2) returned. factorial(3) computes 3 * 2 = 6 and returns.
factorial(3) returned. factorial(4) computes 4 * 6 = 24 and returns.
factorial(4) returned. factorial(5) computes 5 * 24 = 120 and returns.

complexity.note: n calls, each O(1) work; the call stack is n frames deep at the bottom.
